# Systems and Methods for Below-Grade Storage of Spent Nuclear Fuel

## Overview

The present invention provides systems and methods for storing spent nuclear fuel below grade while ensuring adequate ventilation of the storage cavity. By positioning the storage system beneath ground level, the invention offers enhanced protection against environmental and external hazards, while its integrated ventilation design maintains proper thermal management of the stored spent nuclear fuel throughout the storage period.

## System Configuration

The system includes a shell that forms a cavity for receiving a spent nuclear fuel canister, with at least a portion of the shell positioned below grade. The below-grade placement of the shell provides a compact and secure storage arrangement, reducing the above-grade profile of the system and improving overall containment.

To ensure effective ventilation of the storage cavity, the system incorporates at least one inlet ventilation duct that extends from an above-grade inlet to a below-grade outlet located at or near the bottom of the cavity. This configuration draws ambient air from above ground and delivers it to the lower region of the cavity, thereby promoting natural circulation of air around the stored canister and facilitating the removal of decay heat generated by the spent nuclear fuel.

A critical feature of the system is the manner in which the inlet ventilation duct is connected to the shell. Specifically, the duct is joined to the shell such that the cavity is hermetically sealed against the ingress of below-grade fluids. This sealed connection prevents groundwater or other subsurface liquids from entering the storage cavity, protecting the integrity of the spent nuclear fuel canister and maintaining the cleanliness and safety of the storage environment.

## Method of Installation and Use

The method of deploying the system involves several coordinated steps. First, the system is placed within a below-grade hole that has been prepared to receive it. Next, the hole is filled with engineered fill surrounding the system, which provides structural support, stabilization, and additional shielding for the below-grade portion of the shell. Finally, the spent fuel canister is lowered into the cavity, where it is securely housed and continuously ventilated by the integrated inlet ventilation duct.

Together, these systems and methods provide a robust, safe, and thermally efficient solution for the long-term below-grade storage of spent nuclear fuel.

# Systems and Methods for Below-Grade Storage of Spent Nuclear Fuel

## Field of the Invention

The present invention relates generally to the storage of high-level radioactive waste, and more particularly to systems and methods for storing spent nuclear fuel in a below-grade configuration that provides passive ventilation while preventing the ingress of groundwater and other subsurface fluids.

## Background

Spent nuclear fuel remains highly radioactive and thermally active for extended periods following its removal from a reactor core. As such, it must be stored in a manner that provides effective shielding, structural containment, and adequate cooling to dissipate the residual decay heat generated by the radioactive material. Traditional above-grade storage systems, while functional, present challenges related to security, radiation shielding, and vulnerability to environmental and external hazards.

Below-grade storage offers significant advantages, including enhanced radiation shielding provided by the surrounding soil, improved protection against external threats, and a lower physical profile. However, storing spent nuclear fuel underground introduces the critical challenge of managing the ingress of below-grade fluids, such as groundwater, which could compromise the integrity of the storage system and the safety of the contained materials. At the same time, any effective storage system must provide sufficient ventilation to remove the heat generated by the spent fuel, ensuring that temperatures remain within safe operating limits.

## Summary of the Invention

This disclosure describes systems and methods for storing spent nuclear fuel below grade using a hermetically sealed shell that defines an internal storage cavity. The system incorporates an inlet ventilation duct that extends from an above-grade inlet to a below-grade outlet located at the bottom of the cavity. This configuration provides adequate ventilation of the spent fuel storage cavity while simultaneously preventing the ingress of below-grade fluids, thereby ensuring the safe and effective underground containment of hazardous nuclear materials.

## Detailed Description

The storage system comprises a hermetically sealed shell constructed to be positioned substantially below grade within a subsurface environment. The shell defines an internal cavity configured to receive one or more canisters or containers of spent nuclear fuel. Because the shell is hermetically sealed, it forms a robust barrier that isolates the stored fuel from the surrounding subsurface environment, preventing groundwater, moisture, and other below-grade fluids from entering the storage cavity and coming into contact with the radioactive materials.

To provide the necessary cooling, the system employs a passive ventilation arrangement. An inlet ventilation duct extends from an inlet positioned above grade, downward through or alongside the sealed shell, to an outlet located near the bottom of the internal cavity. Ambient air enters the system through the above-grade inlet and travels through the duct to the below-grade outlet at the base of the cavity. As this cooler air is introduced at the bottom of the cavity, it absorbs heat radiating from the spent fuel canisters. The heated air, being less dense, rises naturally through the cavity by means of thermosiphon action and is subsequently discharged through an outlet, typically located at or near the top of the system.

This chimney-like ventilation flow is driven passively by natural convection, requiring no mechanical blowers, pumps, or external power sources to maintain circulation. Such passive operation enhances the reliability and safety of the system, as cooling continues uninterrupted even in the event of a loss of external power or mechanical failure.

A key advantage of the design lies in the arrangement of the inlet ventilation duct. By routing the duct from an above-grade inlet to a below-grade outlet, the system ensures that air can circulate through the deepest portion of the cavity, where cooling is most needed, while the hermetically sealed shell maintains complete isolation from surrounding fluids. The elevation of the inlet above grade further prevents surface water, precipitation, or flooding from entering the ventilation pathway. In this way, the system achieves effective heat removal without compromising the fluid-tight integrity of the containment structure.

## Advantages

The systems and methods described herein provide several important benefits for the long-term storage of spent nuclear fuel:

- **Enhanced shielding and protection:** The below-grade configuration leverages the surrounding soil to provide additional radiation shielding and physical protection against external hazards.

- **Fluid ingress prevention:** The hermetically sealed shell, combined with the above-grade inlet, prevents groundwater and other subsurface fluids from reaching the stored fuel.

- **Passive cooling:** The inlet ventilation duct enables natural convective airflow through the cavity, dissipating decay heat without reliance on active mechanical systems or external power.

- **Safety and reliability:** The passive, sealed design minimizes the risk of contamination and equipment failure, ensuring the safe and effective containment of hazardous nuclear materials over extended storage periods.

## Conclusion

By integrating a hermetically sealed shell with a strategically routed inlet ventilation duct extending from an above-grade inlet to a below-grade outlet at the bottom of the storage cavity, the disclosed systems and methods achieve a balance between two competing requirements: providing adequate ventilation for heat removal while preventing the ingress of below-grade fluids. This design offers a safe, reliable, and effective solution for the underground storage of spent nuclear fuel and other hazardous radioactive materials.

# Understanding Systems

A system is a collection of interconnected components that work together to achieve a common purpose. Systems exist all around us, from the natural world to the technologies we build and the organizations we create.

## What Defines a System?

At its core, a system has several key characteristics:

- **Components or elements** that make up the whole
- **Relationships** or connections between these parts
- **Boundaries** that separate the system from its environment
- **A purpose or function** that the system serves

## Types of Systems

Systems can be classified in many ways. **Natural systems**, such as ecosystems or the human body, emerge and evolve without deliberate design. **Designed systems**, like computers, transportation networks, or businesses, are created intentionally to fulfill specific goals.

Systems can also be **open**, exchanging energy and information with their surroundings, or **closed**, operating in relative isolation. Most real-world systems are open, constantly interacting with their environment.

## Why Systems Thinking Matters

Systems thinking encourages us to look at the bigger picture rather than isolated parts. When we understand how components interact, we can better predict behavior, solve problems, and anticipate unintended consequences.

For example, changing one element in a system often creates ripple effects throughout. A small adjustment in a supply chain, an ecosystem, or a software application can produce outcomes far beyond the initial change.

## Conclusion

Whether we're studying biology, engineering, economics, or society, the concept of systems helps us make sense of complexity. By recognizing patterns, relationships, and interdependencies, we gain the tools to design, manage, and improve the world around us.

# Patent Abstract

## System and Method for Below-Grade Storage of Spent Nuclear Fuel with Cavity Ventilation

A system and method for storing spent nuclear fuel in a below-grade configuration with passive ventilation of the storage cavity is disclosed. The system comprises a storage cavity extending substantially below grade level, the cavity being defined by a shielded enclosure configured to receive at least one canister containing spent nuclear fuel. The below-grade orientation provides enhanced radiation shielding, improved resistance to seismic events, projectile impacts, and environmental hazards, while presenting a reduced above-grade profile.

The system further comprises a ventilation subsystem configured to establish a natural convection airflow through the storage cavity. In one embodiment, cool ambient air enters the cavity through one or more inlet passages positioned to direct air toward a lower region of the cavity. As the air absorbs decay heat emanating from the spent nuclear fuel canister, the heated air rises and is discharged through one or more outlet passages positioned in an upper region of the enclosure. The resulting thermosiphon effect removes residual decay heat from the canister without reliance on active mechanical components, electrical power, or operator intervention.

In certain embodiments, the inlet and outlet passages are configured in a labyrinthine or tortuous geometry to attenuate radiation streaming while permitting substantially unobstructed airflow. The method includes positioning a loaded canister within the below-grade cavity, sealing an upper closure over the cavity, and passively circulating ambient air through the cavity to maintain the canister and stored fuel below prescribed temperature limits. The system thereby provides safe, long-term, passively-cooled storage of spent nuclear fuel while minimizing above-grade structures and enhancing protection against natural and man-made threats.

# Summary of the Invention

The present invention provides an underground storage apparatus for spent nuclear fuel that achieves passive convective cooling of stored fuel canisters while maintaining a hermetically sealed storage cavity that protects the stored fuel from intrusion by groundwater and other subsurface moisture.

In one aspect, the apparatus comprises an elongated storage cavity disposed substantially below grade and configured to receive one or more sealed canisters containing spent nuclear fuel. The storage cavity is defined by a fluid-impermeable containment structure that hermetically isolates the interior of the cavity from the surrounding subgrade environment, thereby preventing ingress of groundwater into the cavity irrespective of the local water table elevation.

In a further aspect, the apparatus includes at least one inlet ventilation duct and at least one outlet ventilation passage arranged to establish a natural convective airflow circuit. Ambient cooling air is drawn through the inlet ventilation duct, directed into thermal communication with the exterior of the sealed canister, heated by decay heat emanating from the spent nuclear fuel, and discharged through the outlet ventilation passage. Because the density of the heated air is reduced relative to the incoming ambient air, the airflow circuit is driven by buoyancy without reliance on active blowers, pumps, or other powered equipment.

Significantly, the ventilation airflow circuit is configured such that the cooling air remains segregated from, and does not enter, the hermetically sealed storage cavity that houses the fuel canister. In certain embodiments, the inlet ventilation duct directs the cooling air along an exterior surface of the containment structure, or through one or more dedicated flow annuli or channels that are physically isolated from the sealed cavity interior. In this manner, the invention decouples the thermal management function of the apparatus from the moisture-exclusion function, permitting robust passive cooling while ensuring that neither ventilation air nor groundwater can compromise the sealed environment surrounding the stored fuel.

In additional aspects, the inlet ventilation duct and outlet ventilation passage may be provided with baffles, screens, filters, or tortuous flow paths that inhibit the entry of debris, precipitation, flooding water, and radiological release, while continuing to permit convective air exchange. The containment structure may further comprise redundant sealing barriers, corrosion-resistant liners, and monitoring provisions to verify the continued integrity of the hermetic seal over an extended storage service life.

Accordingly, embodiments of the present invention provide an underground spent nuclear fuel storage apparatus that combines the safety and security advantages of below-grade emplacement, the reliability of passive convective cooling by means of inlet ventilation ducts, and the long-term protection afforded by a storage cavity that is hermetically sealed against groundwater intrusion.

# Summary of Invention: Below-Grade Spent Nuclear Fuel Storage Apparatus

## System Aspects

The invention is an apparatus for storing canisters of spent nuclear fuel in a **below-grade shell** (a vertical cavity enclosure positioned largely underground). Key structural components typically include:

- **An outer shell/container** installed within an excavated hole or cavity in the ground, extending below grade level to provide radiation shielding using the surrounding earth.
- **An internal storage cavity** sized to receive and hold a sealed canister containing spent nuclear fuel.
- **A lid or closure system** at the top (near grade level) that seals the storage cavity while permitting controlled airflow.
- **Ventilation passages** designed to allow natural convection (passive) cooling of the heat-generating canister without requiring active mechanical systems.
- **Air inlet and outlet ducts** configured so cool ambient air enters low, absorbs decay heat from the canister, and rises to exit—while shielding designs prevent direct radiation streaming (line-of-sight) through the vents.

## Ventilation Method

The system relies on **passive convective cooling**:
1. Cooler ambient air is drawn in through inlet openings.
2. Air flows around the hot canister, absorbing decay heat.
3. Heated air rises and is discharged through outlet openings.
4. This continuous natural circulation removes heat without pumps or fans, enhancing reliability and safety.

## Method Aspects (Installation & Operation)

The installation method generally involves:
- **Excavating a hole** in the ground to the required depth.
- **Positioning the shell** into the hole so that the majority of the structure sits below grade.
- **Securing/anchoring** the shell (often in a concrete foundation or surrounding fill) for stability and additional shielding.
- **Lowering a sealed canister** of spent fuel into the internal cavity.
- **Installing the closure lid** and establishing the ventilation pathways.
- **Operating** the storage unit via passive air cooling over the long-term storage period.

## Key Advantages
- Below-grade placement uses **soil as natural shielding**, reducing radiation exposure.
- **Passive ventilation** eliminates active cooling dependencies.
- Improved **seismic stability** and lower profile compared to fully above-ground casks.

---

# Ventilated Underground Storage System for Spent Nuclear Fuel Canisters

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates generally to systems for the interim dry storage of spent nuclear fuel, and more particularly to a below-grade ventilated storage module adapted to receive a sealed spent fuel canister, wherein passive convective airflow provides decay heat removal while an engineered barrier system substantially isolates the stored canister from below-grade fluid intrusion.

## BACKGROUND

Spent nuclear fuel discharged from a reactor continues to generate substantial decay heat and ionizing radiation for extended periods. Above-grade storage casks are known in the art but present concerns relating to seismic overturning, aircraft impact vulnerability, and radiological shine to unrestricted areas. A need exists for a storage system that recesses the stored canister below the surrounding grade while maintaining reliable passive cooling and protection against groundwater and other below-grade fluids.

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

In accordance with one aspect of the invention, there is provided a ventilated underground storage system comprising: (a) an elongate storage shell defining an internal cavity; (b) a ventilation duct arrangement establishing at least one inlet flow path and at least one outlet flow path in thermal communication with said cavity; (c) a sealing arrangement disposed about a lower and lateral extent of said shell and adapted to resist infiltration of below-grade fluids; and (d) an engineered fill medium disposed in supporting relation about said shell.

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION

### The Storage Shell

In a preferred embodiment, the storage shell comprises a generally cylindrical, vertically-oriented tubular member fabricated from carbon steel, said member having a closed lower end and an open upper end configured to receive a spent fuel canister lowered substantially coaxially therein. The shell defines an annular clearance between an inner wall of the shell and an outer wall of the received canister, said annular clearance constituting a primary flow annulus for cooling air.

The lower end of the shell may terminate in a base plate supported upon a reinforced concrete foundation pad, said base plate optionally incorporating standoff features or a pedestal to establish a plenum beneath the canister and to promote distribution of inlet air about the lower canister region. An upper closure lid, providing radiological shielding and physical protection, is removably seated upon the open upper end.

Radiological shielding is provided in cooperation with the surrounding subgrade and, in certain embodiments, by a concrete overpack or shielding ring surrounding an upper portion of the shell in the vicinity of the ventilation penetrations.

### Ventilation Duct Routing

The system establishes a passive, buoyancy-driven ventilation circuit requiring no forced-air equipment during normal operation. Cooling airflow is induced by the density differential between ambient inlet air and heated air within the flow annulus, in accordance with thermosiphon principles.

In the described arrangement, one or more inlet ducts communicate ambient air from an above-grade intake, downwardly along a routed path, to a lower plenum region beneath or adjacent the received canister. Each inlet duct is preferably routed with at least one directional offset—for example, a serpentine or labyrinthine bend—such that no straight-line radiation streaming path exists between the stored canister and the exterior environment, thereby attenuating radiological shine while preserving flow area.

Air admitted to the lower plenum rises through the flow annulus, absorbs decay heat from the canister surface, and is discharged through one or more outlet ducts communicating with an above-grade exhaust opening disposed at an elevation above the inlet, so as to maximize the effective chimney height and resulting draft. The inlet and outlet intakes are provided with screens, louvers, or debris guards to inhibit ingress of precipitation, wildlife, and foreign matter, while permitting substantially unobstructed airflow.

### Sealing Against Below-Grade Fluids

To resist infiltration of groundwater, surface water percolating through the subgrade, and other below-grade fluids into the shell cavity or the ventilation circuit, the system incorporates a multi-component sealing arrangement.

The exterior surfaces of the shell in contact with the surrounding subgrade may be treated with a corrosion-resistant coating, membrane, or cathodic protection system. A continuous waterproof barrier—such as a bituminous, elastomeric, or geomembrane layer—may be disposed about the lateral and lower extents of the shell or its supporting foundation to divert fluid away from the cavity.

The ventilation penetrations, which represent potential fluid entry points, are elevated and configured such that their below-grade routing is sealed at each interface where a duct passes through a structural boundary, for example by means of gasketed flanges, welded penetration collars, or grouted sleeve connections. Drainage provisions—such as a graded base and a sump or drain channel in communication with the lower plenum—may be provided to collect and remove any incidental moisture, thereby preventing accumulation against the canister.

### Installation Method Using Engineered Fill

According to a further aspect of the invention, a method of installing the storage system comprises the steps of:

1. **Excavating** a below-grade opening in a host geologic medium to a depth sufficient to receive the storage shell in substantially recessed relation to the surrounding grade;

2. **Placing and compacting a prepared subgrade or foundation pad** at the base of the excavation, said pad being leveled and, in certain embodiments, comprising reinforced concrete adapted to bear the combined load of the shell and canister;

3. **Positioning the storage shell** within the excavation in a substantially vertical orientation upon the foundation pad, and securing the shell against the pad;

4. **Routing and connecting the ventilation ducts** and establishing the sealed penetrations and above-grade intake and exhaust terminations;

5. **Progressively placing an engineered fill medium** into the annular space between the exterior of the shell and the walls of the excavation, said engineered fill being selected and controlled for particle gradation, compaction density, thermal conductivity, and permeability;

6. **Compacting said engineered fill in successive lifts** so as to provide uniform lateral support to the shell, to establish a predictable thermal conduction path to the surrounding geologic medium, and to develop a low-permeability zone that assists in diverting below-grade fluids; and

7. **Completing the installation** by finishing the surrounding grade, installing the upper closure lid and any concrete overpack or shielding, and verifying ventilation flow and radiological performance.

The engineered fill medium is preferably selected to be non-reactive with the shell material and to maintain dimensional and drainage stability under thermal cycling and anticipated seismic loading, whereby the fill cooperates with the sealing arrangement to protect the shell while cooperating with the ventilation circuit to reject decay heat to the environment.

## CLAIMS (ILLUSTRATIVE)

1. A ventilated underground storage system for a spent nuclear fuel canister, comprising: a storage shell defining an internal cavity adapted to receive said canister in spaced relation defining a flow annulus; a passive ventilation arrangement having an inlet duct communicating ambient air to a lower region of said cavity and an outlet duct discharging heated air at an elevation above said inlet, at least one of said ducts being routed to interrupt straight-line radiation streaming; a sealing arrangement disposed about said shell to resist below-grade fluid infiltration; and an engineered fill medium disposed about said shell in laterally supporting and thermally conductive relation.

2. The system of claim 1, wherein said inlet and outlet ducts establish a buoyancy-driven thermosiphon circuit operable without forced air.

3. The system of claim 1, further comprising a drainage provision in communication with a lower plenum of said cavity for removal of incidental moisture.

4. A method of installing the system of claim 1, comprising excavating a below-grade opening, placing a foundation pad, positioning said shell thereon, connecting said ventilation arrangement, and placing and compacting said engineered fill in successive lifts about said shell.

---

*The foregoing description is illustrative of representative embodiments and is not intended to limit the scope of the invention, which may be embodied in various alternative forms within the spirit of the disclosure.*
